CALIFORNIA DENSITY BONUS LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Development LLC · 123 Main St, Springfield

DENSITY BONUS APPLICATION — PROJECT IDENTIFICATION
CALIFORNIA DENSITY BONUS LAW — PROJECT INFORMATION
(Referencing California Government Code Section 65915, the state Density Bonus Law, which requires a city, county, or city and county to grant a density bonus and, where requested, incentives or concessions, waivers or reductions of development standards, and reduced parking ratios to a qualifying housing development in exchange for a share of affordable, senior, or other specified units)

Applicant/Developer: Acme Development LLC
Property Address: 123 Main St, Springfield
Local Agency (city, county, or city and county with land use jurisdiction over the property): City of Springfield
Description of Proposed Housing Development (base number of units, proposed affordability mix, and any land donation, childcare facility, or student/senior housing component): 50-unit development including 5 lower-income units

This sheet identifies the property, the applicant, and the local agency for reference in connection with a request for a density bonus, incentives or concessions, waivers or reductions of development standards, or reduced parking ratios under California's Density Bonus Law. It states facts for identification purposes only; it does not itself constitute or substitute for the density bonus application that must be submitted to, and acted on by, the local agency, and it does not determine whether the proposed development qualifies for a density bonus, a particular number of incentives or concessions, or any waiver under any specific provision of Section 65915.

ELIGIBILITY THRESHOLDS TRIGGERING THE DENSITY BONUS ENTITLEMENT
Under California's Density Bonus Law, a city, county, or city and county must grant one density bonus, in the amount specified by the statute's sliding-scale calculation, and, if requested by the applicant, incentives or concessions, waivers or reductions of development standards, and reduced parking ratios, to an applicant who seeks and agrees to construct a housing development that contains at least one of several statutorily specified thresholds. Two of the most commonly used thresholds are that at least ten percent of the total units be for rental or sale to lower income households, or that at least five percent of the total units be for rental or sale to very low income households, with the applicable income categories cross-referenced to the Health and Safety Code. Other listed thresholds address senior citizen housing developments, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth, disabled veteran, and homeless housing, and 100-percent-affordable developments, each triggering its own density bonus percentage under a separate subdivision of the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A city, county, or city and county shall grant one density bonus, the amount of which shall be as specified in subdivision (f), and, if requested by the applicant and consistent with the applicable requirements of this section, incentives or concessions, as described in subdivision (d), waivers or reductions of development standards, as described in subdivision (e), and parking ratios, as described in subdivision (p), if an applicant for a housing development seeks and agrees to construct a housing development, excluding any units permitted by the density bonus awarded pursuant to this section, that will contain at least any one of the following:"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(b)(1), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (b)(1) (density bonus entitlement) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the operative grant-of-entitlement sentence and the two most commonly used percentage thresholds (lower income and very low income rental/sale units) out of at least seven alternative qualifying thresholds enumerated in the same subdivision (including senior housing, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth or disabled veteran housing, homeless shelters, and 100-percent-affordable developments); it does not reproduce the detailed eligibility conditions attached to those other thresholds, each of which has its own cross-referenced definitions and, in some cases, its own density bonus percentage schedule addressed in other clauses of this document. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

TWO COMMON QUALIFYING SET-ASIDES: LOWER INCOME AND VERY LOW INCOME UNITS
Among the statutory thresholds that qualify a housing development for a density bonus, California law specifies that at least ten percent of a development's total units, including a shared housing building development, dedicated to rental or sale to lower income households (as defined by cross-reference to the Health and Safety Code) will qualify the development for the entitlement described elsewhere in the statute. Alternatively, at least five percent of the total units dedicated to rental or sale to very low income households (also cross-referenced to the Health and Safety Code) will independently qualify a development. These are minimum set-aside percentages; a development that dedicates a higher percentage of units to either income category receives a correspondingly larger density bonus under the statute's sliding-scale calculation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(A) Ten percent of the total units of a housing development, including a shared housing building development, for rental or sale to lower income households, as defined in Section 50079.5 of the Health and Safety Code. (B) Five percent of the total units of a housing development, including a shared housing building development, for rental or sale to very low income households, as defined in Section 50105 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(b)(1)(A)-(B), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (b)(1)(A) and (B) (lower income and very low income unit thresholds) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the lower income and very low income rental/sale thresholds; it does not reproduce the separate, differently worded thresholds for senior housing developments, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth or disabled veteran housing, homeless shelters, or 100-percent-affordable developments, each of which is defined in the same subdivision but is not quoted here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

HOW THE DENSITY BONUS PERCENTAGE IS CALCULATED
California's Density Bonus Law defines a “density bonus” as a density increase over the otherwise maximum allowable gross residential density under the local zoning ordinance in effect as of the date of the applicant's application, or, if the applicant elects, a lesser percentage of density increase, including no increase in density at all. The amount of density increase to which an applicant is entitled is not fixed; it varies according to how far the percentage of affordable housing units in the development exceeds the minimum percentage thresholds described elsewhere in the statute. The statute sets out separate sliding-scale tables tying specific affordable-unit percentages to specific density bonus percentages, with the tables differing depending on which income category (lower income, very low income, or moderate income) and which qualifying category (e.g., standard rental/sale development, 100-percent-affordable development, or land-donation development) applies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the purposes of this chapter, “density bonus” means a density increase over the otherwise maximum allowable gross residential density, as of the date of application by the applicant to the city, county, or city and county, or, if elected by the applicant, a lesser percentage of density increase, including, but not limited to, no increase in density. The amount of density increase to which the applicant is entitled shall vary according to the amount by which the percentage of affordable housing units exceeds the percentage established in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(f), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (f) (definition and variable entitlement of the density bonus) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the general definitional and variable-entitlement language that introduces the density bonus calculation; it does not reproduce the numeric sliding-scale tables themselves (which pair specific affordable-unit percentages, such as 10 percent low-income units, with specific density bonus percentages, such as 20 percent, ranging up to a 50-percent maximum bonus under the standard tables, or up to an 80-percent bonus for certain 100-percent-affordable developments), nor the additional density bonus available under a separate 2025 amendment (subdivision (v)) for developments that combine several affordability tiers. Local zoning specifics vary by jurisdiction and are not addressed here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

ENTITLEMENT TO INCENTIVES OR CONCESSIONS AND THE NARROW GROUNDS FOR DENIAL
An applicant for a density bonus may submit to the local government a proposal for specific incentives or concessions and may request a meeting to discuss it. California law requires the local government to grant the requested concession or incentive unless it makes a written finding, supported by substantial evidence, that the concession or incentive would not result in identifiable and actual cost reductions for affordable housing costs or targeted-unit rents, would have a specific adverse impact on public health or safety or on a listed historical resource without a feasible mitigation, or would be contrary to state or federal law. The number of incentives or concessions to which an applicant is entitled increases with the percentage of affordable units the development includes, on a tiered scale set out in the statute, up to five incentives or concessions for developments meeting the criteria for 100-percent-affordable projects.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The city, county, or city and county shall grant the concession or incentive requested by the applicant unless the city, county, or city and county makes a written finding, based upon substantial evidence, of any of the following:"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(d)(1)-(2), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (d), paragraphs (1) (denial standard) and (2)(A)-(B) (incentive/concession count) -- these two paragraphs of the same subdivision are cited together and are not independent of each other (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  "(A) One incentive or concession for projects that include at least 10 percent of the total units for lower income households, at least 5 percent for very low income households, or at least 10 percent for persons and families of moderate income in a development in which the units are for sale. (B) Two incentives or concessions for projects that include at least 17 percent of the total units for lower income households, at least 10 percent for very low income households, or at least 20 percent for persons and families of moderate income in a development in which the units are for sale."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(d)(2)(A)-(B), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (d)(2)(A) and (B) (first two tiers of the incentive/concession count schedule) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the denial-standard sentence and the first two tiers of the incentive/concession count schedule (one incentive for a 10-percent lower income or 5-percent very low income set-aside; two incentives for 17-percent lower income or 10-percent very low income); it does not reproduce the third tier, the five-incentive tier for 100-percent-affordable projects, or the further, more generous tiers added by 2025 legislation for projects combining moderate-income and very low or lower income units (subdivision (b)(1)(v)). (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

WHAT COUNTS AS AN “INCENTIVE OR CONCESSION”
California's Density Bonus Law defines “concession or incentive” to include a reduction in site development standards or a modification of zoning code or architectural design requirements that exceed minimum state building standards -- such as a reduction in setback, square footage, or parking requirements -- where the reduction results in identifiable and actual cost reductions for affordable housing costs or targeted-unit rents. The statute also lists approval of mixed-use zoning alongside the housing project, where the non-residential use will reduce the housing development's cost and is compatible with the surrounding area, and a third, catch-all category of other regulatory incentives or concessions proposed by the developer or the local government that result in identifiable, actual cost reductions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the purposes of this chapter, concession or incentive means any of the following: (1) A reduction in site development standards or a modification of zoning code requirements or architectural design requirements that exceed the minimum building standards approved by the California Building Standards Commission as provided in Part 2.5 (commencing with Section 18901) of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code, including, but not limited to, a reduction in setback and square footage requirements and in the ratio of vehicular parking spaces that would otherwise be required that results in identifiable and actual cost reductions, to provide for affordable housing costs, as defined in Section 50052.5 of the Health and Safety Code, or for rents for the targeted units to be set as specified in subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(k)(1), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (k), introductory clause and paragraph (1) (definition of concession or incentive) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the first enumerated category (site development standard reductions) in full and summarizes, without quoting, the mixed-use and catch-all categories that follow it in the same subdivision; the statute's full text of those remaining categories, and the separate additional incentives available for childcare facilities and 100-percent-affordable projects addressed in other subdivisions, are not reproduced here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

WAIVER OR REDUCTION OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS THAT WOULD PRECLUDE CONSTRUCTION
Separate from the incentive-or-concession process, California law prohibits a local government from applying any development standard that would have the effect of physically precluding construction of a density-bonus-eligible development at the densities, or with the concessions or incentives, permitted by the statute. An applicant may submit a proposal for the waiver or reduction of such a development standard and may request a meeting with the local government. The statute makes this waiver process distinct from the incentive/concession count: a request for a waiver or reduction of development standards neither reduces nor increases the number of incentives or concessions to which the applicant is separately entitled. If a court finds that a local government's refusal to grant a waiver or reduction violates the statute, the statute directs the court to award the prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs of suit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In no case may a city, county, or city and county apply any development standard that will have the effect of physically precluding the construction of a development meeting the criteria of subdivision (b) at the densities or with the concessions or incentives permitted by this section."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(e)(1), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (e)(1) (no-preclusion rule for development standards) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses the general no-preclusion rule; it does not reproduce the statute's separate carve-outs limiting the waiver obligation where a waiver would have a specific, adverse impact on public health or safety without a feasible mitigation, would adversely affect a listed historical resource, or would be contrary to state or federal law, nor the narrower eligibility rule that applies to a development that has already received a waiver from maximum density controls under a cross-referenced clause of subdivision (f). (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

STATUTORY CAPS ON PARKING RATIOS FOR DENSITY BONUS DEVELOPMENTS
Upon a developer's request, California law caps the vehicular parking ratio a local government may impose on a qualifying density bonus development, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests. The default statutory caps are one onsite parking space for a unit with zero to one bedroom, one and one-half onsite spaces for a unit with two to three bedrooms, and two and one-half spaces for a unit with four or more bedrooms. The statute further reduces these caps for developments that include a higher percentage of low-income or very low income units and are located within one-half mile of a major transit stop with unobstructed access, and it sets a separate, distinct cap for single bedspaces in student housing developments.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "upon the request of the developer, a city, county, or city and county shall not require a vehicular parking ratio, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests, of a development meeting the criteria of subdivisions (b) and (c), that exceeds the following ratios: (A) Zero to one bedroom: one onsite parking space. (B) Two to three bedrooms: one and one-half onsite parking spaces. (C) Four and more bedrooms: two and one-half parking spaces."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(p)(1), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (p)(1) (default parking ratio caps) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the default parking ratio caps for zero-to-one, two-to-three, and four-or-more bedroom units; it does not reproduce the statute's additional, more restrictive 0.5-spaces-per-unit and 0.5-spaces-per-bedroom caps for developments near major transit stops, the zero-parking rule for student housing bedspaces, or the separate exceptions in paragraphs (3) and (4) of the same subdivision for special circumstances. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

ADDITIONAL DENSITY BONUS FOR DONATING LAND TO THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT
Separate from the affordable-unit density bonus, California law provides an additional density bonus for an applicant who, in connection with a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval, donates land to the local government in accordance with the statute's conditions. A qualifying land donation entitles the applicant to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development, with the percentage increasing on a sliding scale as the proportion of very low income units the donated land will support increases, up to a 35-percent maximum combined density increase when the land-donation bonus is combined with the standard affordable-unit bonus.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "When an applicant for a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval donates land to a city, county, or city and county in accordance with this subdivision, the applicant shall be entitled to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development"
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(g)(1), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (g)(1) (land donation density bonus) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the introductory sentence establishing the 15-percent baseline land-donation bonus and its sliding-scale structure; it does not reproduce the statute's detailed eligibility conditions for a qualifying land donation (including the required timing of the transfer, the minimum developable acreage and zoning classification of the donated land, and its required proximity to the development it serves), which are set out in subsequent, unquoted subparagraphs of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

REQUIRED DURATION OF CONTINUED AFFORDABILITY
In exchange for the density bonus, California law requires an applicant to agree to, and requires the local government to ensure, the continued affordability of the very low income and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus for a period of 55 years, or for a longer period if a construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program applicable to the development requires it. The statute separately addresses the rent levels that must be set for those units and, in a different paragraph of the same subdivision, the conditions that apply to for-sale units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An applicant shall agree to, and the city, county, or city and county shall ensure, the continued affordability of all very low and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the award of the density bonus for 55 years or a longer period of time if required by the construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(c)(1)(A), California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (c)(1)(A) (55-year affordability covenant) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=65915.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the 55-year affordability duration rule for rental units; it does not reproduce the statute's separate rent-setting formula for lower income density bonus units (including the modified rent structure that applies to 100-percent-affordable developments) or the distinct resale-price and equity-sharing conditions that apply to for-sale density bonus units under a different paragraph of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE
ACKNOWLEDGMENT

This document is an informational summary of California's Density Bonus Law (Government Code Section 65915) as it relates to the identified property and applicant. It describes generally applicable statutory rules regarding density bonuses, incentives and concessions, waivers of development standards, parking ratio caps, land donation bonuses, and affordability covenant duration. It does not determine the specific density bonus percentage, number of incentives or concessions, or waivers to which any particular development is entitled, does not reflect any local agency's implementing ordinance or its procedures, and is not a substitute for consulting the applicable local agency or a licensed attorney about a specific project.

Applicant/Developer Signature: _______________________________________________
Printed Name: Acme Development LLC
Date: September 1, 2026
City, State: Oakland, California

citations.quote: For the purposes of this chapter, concession or incentive means any of the following: (1) A reduction in site development standards or a modification of zoning code requirements or architectural design requirements that exceed the minimum building standards approved by the California Building Standards Commission as provided in Part 2.5 (commencing with Section 18901) of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code, including, but not limited to, a reduction in setback and square footage requirements and in the ratio of vehicular parking spaces that would otherwise be required that results in identifiable and actual cost reductions, to provide for affordable housing costs, as defined in Section 50052.5 of the Health and Safety Code, or for rents for the targeted units to be set as specified in subdivision (c).

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only the first enumerated category (site development standard reductions) in full and summarizes, without quoting, the mixed-use and catch-all categories that follow it in the same subdivision; the statute's full text of those remaining categories, and the separate additional incentives available for childcare facilities and 100-percent-affordable projects addressed in other subdivisions, are not reproduced here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

expectedJSON.body: Separate from the incentive-or-concession process, California law prohibits a local government from applying any development standard that would have the effect of physically precluding construction of a density-bonus-eligible development at the densities, or with the concessions or incentives, permitted by the statute. An applicant may submit a proposal for the waiver or reduction of such a development standard and may request a meeting with the local government. The statute makes this waiver process distinct from the incentive/concession count: a request for a waiver or reduction of development standards neither reduces nor increases the number of incentives or concessions to which the applicant is separately entitled. If a court finds that a local government's refusal to grant a waiver or reduction violates the statute, the statute directs the court to award the prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs of suit.

citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (e)(1) (no-preclusion rule for development standards)
citations.quote: In no case may a city, county, or city and county apply any development standard that will have the effect of physically precluding the construction of a development meeting the criteria of subdivision (b) at the densities or with the concessions or incentives permitted by this section.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause addresses the general no-preclusion rule; it does not reproduce the statute's separate carve-outs limiting the waiver obligation where a waiver would have a specific, adverse impact on public health or safety without a feasible mitigation, would adversely affect a listed historical resource, or would be contrary to state or federal law, nor the narrower eligibility rule that applies to a development that has already received a waiver from maximum density controls under a cross-referenced clause of subdivision (f). (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

expectedJSON.body: Upon a developer's request, California law caps the vehicular parking ratio a local government may impose on a qualifying density bonus development, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests. The default statutory caps are one onsite parking space for a unit with zero to one bedroom, one and one-half onsite spaces for a unit with two to three bedrooms, and two and one-half spaces for a unit with four or more bedrooms. The statute further reduces these caps for developments that include a higher percentage of low-income or very low income units and are located within one-half mile of a major transit stop with unobstructed access, and it sets a separate, distinct cap for single bedspaces in student housing developments.

citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (p)(1) (default parking ratio caps)
citations.quote: upon the request of the developer, a city, county, or city and county shall not require a vehicular parking ratio, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests, of a development meeting the criteria of subdivisions (b) and (c), that exceeds the following ratios: (A) Zero to one bedroom: one onsite parking space. (B) Two to three bedrooms: one and one-half onsite parking spaces. (C) Four and more bedrooms: two and one-half parking spaces.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only the default parking ratio caps for zero-to-one, two-to-three, and four-or-more bedroom units; it does not reproduce the statute's additional, more restrictive 0.5-spaces-per-unit and 0.5-spaces-per-bedroom caps for developments near major transit stops, the zero-parking rule for student housing bedspaces, or the separate exceptions in paragraphs (3) and (4) of the same subdivision for special circumstances. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

expectedJSON.body: Separate from the affordable-unit density bonus, California law provides an additional density bonus for an applicant who, in connection with a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval, donates land to the local government in accordance with the statute's conditions. A qualifying land donation entitles the applicant to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development, with the percentage increasing on a sliding scale as the proportion of very low income units the donated land will support increases, up to a 35-percent maximum combined density increase when the land-donation bonus is combined with the standard affordable-unit bonus.

citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (g)(1) (land donation density bonus)
citations.quote: When an applicant for a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval donates land to a city, county, or city and county in accordance with this subdivision, the applicant shall be entitled to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only the introductory sentence establishing the 15-percent baseline land-donation bonus and its sliding-scale structure; it does not reproduce the statute's detailed eligibility conditions for a qualifying land donation (including the required timing of the transfer, the minimum developable acreage and zoning classification of the donated land, and its required proximity to the development it serves), which are set out in subsequent, unquoted subparagraphs of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

expectedJSON.body: In exchange for the density bonus, California law requires an applicant to agree to, and requires the local government to ensure, the continued affordability of the very low income and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus for a period of 55 years, or for a longer period if a construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program applicable to the development requires it. The statute separately addresses the rent levels that must be set for those units and, in a different paragraph of the same subdivision, the conditions that apply to for-sale units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus.

citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (c)(1)(A) (55-year affordability covenant)
citations.quote: An applicant shall agree to, and the city, county, or city and county shall ensure, the continued affordability of all very low and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the award of the density bonus for 55 years or a longer period of time if required by the construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause addresses only the 55-year affordability duration rule for rental units; it does not reproduce the statute's separate rent-setting formula for lower income density bonus units (including the modified rent structure that applies to 100-percent-affordable developments) or the distinct resale-price and equity-sharing conditions that apply to for-sale density bonus units under a different paragraph of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)
